```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Topological Relational Class Analysis (tRCA) recovers three things from
attitudinal survey data in one step:

- **positions**: groups of respondents (factions) who answer the items in a
  similar way;
- **construals**: which positions are relevant to one another, that is, who
  is "playing the same game";
- **topology**: how the positions relate within each game, whether aligned,
  opposed, or orthogonal.

tRCA treats the survey as a signed network between respondents and items,
embeds both in a shared spectral space, and clusters the respondents. A
signed block density matrix then summarizes how the factions relate.
Relational Class Analysis (RCA; Goldberg 2011) is included as a baseline.

This vignette walks through one analysis: simulate data with a known
structure, fit tRCA, read the topology, and compare the result with RCA.

```{r load}
library(trca)
```

## Simulated data with a known topology

`sim_triadic_impasse()` generates three factions, each of which favors its
own block of items and rejects the other two. Every pair of factions is
therefore opposed: a "triadic impasse". The `truth` element records each
respondent's faction.

```{r simulate}
sim <- sim_triadic_impasse(n_per_faction = 60, items_per_block = 4, seed = 1)
dim(sim$data)
```

The package also simulates bipolar opposition (`sim_bipolar()`), consensus
(`sim_consensus()`), hub-and-spoke (`sim_hub_and_spoke()`), multipolar
opposition (`sim_multipolar()`), and coalitions (`sim_coalition()`).

Before fitting, `check_data()` reports missing values, constant
respondents or items, the response scale, and a suggested centering.

```{r check}
check_data(sim$data)
```

## Fitting tRCA

```{r fit}
fit <- trca(sim$data, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

`trca()` chose the number of factions automatically (see
[Choosing the number of factions](#choosing-the-number-of-factions)). It
recovers the simulated factions exactly:

```{r recovery}
table(estimated = fit$clusters, true = sim$truth)
adjusted_rand_index(fit$clusters, sim$truth)
```

The two most useful arguments besides `k` are:

- `centering`: `"mean"` (the default) centers each item on its mean, so a
  positive value means "more than the average respondent". `"midpoint"`
  centers on the scale midpoint (for example 3 on a 1-5 scale), so a
  positive value means "agree". Midpoint centering is easier to interpret
  when the scale has a meaningful neutral point.
- `seed`: k-means uses random starts. Pass a seed to make a fit
  reproducible. Without one, results can differ slightly between runs.

## Reading the topology

`topology()` computes the signed block density matrix `B` and classifies it.
Each entry is the correlation between two factions' mean response
profiles: positive means the factions are aligned, negative means opposed,
and near zero means orthogonal (they disagree about different things, or
not at all).

```{r topology}
topo <- topology(fit)
topo
```

Factions joined by substantive ties (|B| above `tie_threshold`, 0.1 by
default) form a **game**. Each game is classified into one of: Consensus,
Bipolar Opposition, Triadic Impasse, Multipolar Opposition, Coalition,
Hub-and-Spoke, or Complex. Here all three factions oppose each other, so the
data form a single Triadic Impasse.

Factions can be given substantive names once you have inspected them:

```{r name}
topo <- name_factions(topo, c("Left", "Centre", "Right"))
round(topo$B, 2)
```

## Plotting

The plotting functions use ggplot2 (a suggested package) and return ggplot
objects that can be modified further.

The block matrix as a heatmap:

```{r plot-block, eval = has_ggplot}
plot_block_matrix(topo)
```

The same relations as a network. Edge color shows the sign (blue for
opposition, red for alignment) and edge width shows the strength:

```{r plot-network, eval = has_ggplot}
plot_faction_network(topo)
```

Each faction's mean response to each item, relative to the overall mean,
shows what the factions agree and disagree about:

```{r plot-profiles, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 5}
plot_faction_profiles(sim$data, fit$clusters, topo = topo)
```

The joint embedding of respondents (points) and items (labels) in the first
two dimensions:

```{r plot-embedding, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit)
```

## Which items matter

`trca_item_diagnostics()` reports, for each item, its variance, its norm in
the embedding (how strongly it shapes the solution), and its eta-squared
(how much of its variance the factions explain).

```{r items}
items <- trca_item_diagnostics(fit, sim$data)
head(items[, c("item", "item_var", "embedding_norm", "eta_sq")])
```

With many items, `trca(..., filter_items = TRUE)` drops items whose
embedding norm is below average before clustering. The screening uses only
the embedding, not the clusters, so it does not bias the result towards
the factions it finds.

## Comparison with RCA

RCA builds a respondent-by-respondent network from the *absolute*
correlations between respondents' answers. Taking absolute values means two
respondents who answer in mirror-image ways look just as similar as two who
answer identically, so opposed positions are merged. `compare_methods()`
fits both and reads both topologies from the same block density measure:

```{r compare}
compare_methods(sim$data, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

RCA finds two groups instead of three: it puts one faction together with
most of another, even though the two oppose each other, and so reports a
bipolar structure. Cross-tabulating against the truth shows this:

```{r rca-table}
rca <- rca_baseline(sim$data, seed = 1)
table(rca = rca$clusters, true = sim$truth)
```

`rca_baseline()` (spectral clustering) and `rca_leiden()` (Leiden community
detection) fit RCA directly.

## Choosing the number of factions

When `k` is not supplied, `trca()` chooses it in two steps.

1. **Is there more than one faction?** Parallel analysis counts the
   dimensions of the data that carry more structure than shuffled data
   would. The gap statistic then checks whether respondents form separate
   groups along those dimensions or one continuous spread. If they form one
   spread, `trca()` returns a single faction (Consensus).
2. **How many factions?** Otherwise, the silhouette criterion chooses k,
   using only as many embedding dimensions as parallel analysis found (k
   factions span k - 1 dimensions).

Both steps are recorded in the fit:

```{r k-diagnostics}
fit$k_method
fit$signal_dims
```

On consensus data, where everyone shares one profile with varying intensity,
the first step returns one faction:

```{r consensus}
cons <- sim_consensus(n = 120, seed = 2)
fit_cons <- trca(cons$data, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit_cons$k
fit_cons$one_faction_test$one_faction
topology(fit_cons)
```

To see the evidence across a range of k, `trca_select_k()` reports the
automatic choice with its silhouette widths, alongside the eigengap, the
within-cluster sum of squares, and a spectral BIC:

```{r select-k}
ks <- trca_select_k(sim$data, k_range = 2:8, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
ks
```

The spectral BIC penalizes each extra faction in proportion to the largest
k considered, so in small samples it can prefer too few factions. Here it
picks 2 when `k_range` runs to 8; with `k_range = 2:6` it picks 3. Treat it
as a secondary diagnostic.

You can always set `k` yourself, for example to match theory or a previous
analysis, or set `min_k = 2` to skip the single-faction test.

## Using your own data

`trca()` takes a matrix or data frame with one row per respondent and one
column per item. Some practical points:

- **Item types.** Numeric and logical columns are used as they are. Ordered
  factors are converted to their integer codes. Columns imported with haven
  keep their numeric codes. Unordered factors and character columns are
  rejected, because their codes have no order.
- **Missing-data codes.** Survey files often code "refused" or "don't know"
  as negative numbers (for example -9). Recode these to `NA` first;
  `check_data()` warns about negative values in labelled columns.
- **Missing values.** `NA` responses are allowed. tRCA treats a missing
  response as the absence of a tie between that respondent and that item.
  Respondents or items with no responses at all must be removed.
- **Mixed scales.** By default (`rescale = TRUE`) each item is rescaled to
  0-1, so items on 1-3 and 1-7 scales contribute equally.

A typical analysis looks like this:

```{r own-data, eval = FALSE}
library(haven)
survey <- read_dta("survey.dta")
items <- survey[, c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5", "q6")]
items[] <- lapply(items, function(x) replace(x, x < 0, NA))

check_data(items)
fit <- trca(items, centering = "midpoint", seed = 1)
topo <- topology(fit)
plot_faction_network(topo)
```

## References

Goldberg, A. (2011). Mapping shared understandings using relational class
analysis: The case of the cultural omnivore reexamined. *American Journal
of Sociology*, 116(5), 1397-1436. doi:10.1086/657976

Sotoudeh, R. From typology to topology: Positions, construals, and
relational structure in attitudinal data. Forthcoming.
